title: The microscope and the rules of working with it. Preparing temporary slides. Viruses. Prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells, their structure and differences

goals.text: To teach the student the tasks of biology and the main properties of life, the cell theory, the structure of the light and electron microscope and the rules of working with them, the technique of preparing a temporary slide, and the structure and medical importance of the non-cellular (viruses) and cellular (prokaryotic and eukaryotic) forms of life.
By the end of the class the student should know:

items: the main properties of life and its levels of organization;
the main statements of the cell theory and the methods of studying the cell;
the mechanical, optical and illuminating parts of the light microscope and the types of microscopes;
the structure and reproduction of viruses and bacteriophages and the diseases they cause;
the main differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells.

goals.text: The student should be able to:

items: set up the microscope and examine a slide under the low-power and high-power objective;
calculate the total magnification;
prepare a temporary slide (onion skin epidermis);
recognize and correct mistakes made while working with the microscope.

sections.title: 1. Biology and the main properties of life

blocks.text: **Biology** (Greek *bios* — life, *logos* — science) is the science that studies all manifestations of life: the structure, function, development and origin of organisms and their relationships with each other and with the environment. The term was introduced independently by J.B. Lamarck and G. Treviranus at the beginning of the XIX century. **Medical biology** studies the human body as a biological object and is the foundation for histology, physiology, biochemistry, microbiology, pathology and the clinical sciences.

Biology uses **observation, description, comparison, experiment, the historical method, modeling** and **statistical** methods. Living nature differs from non-living nature by the following set of properties:

blocks.title: Table 1.1. The main properties of life
head: Property
Meaning
rows: Based on proteins and nucleic acids; rich in the organogenic elements C, H, O, N
Homeostasis — keeping the internal environment constant
Constant replacement of the component parts
Passing traits to the next generation and producing new traits
Responding to external and internal stimuli
The organism consists of separate parts but works as a single system

blocks.text: Levels of organization of life

items: **Molecular-genetic** — nucleic acids and proteins; storing and transmitting hereditary information.
**Cellular** — the cell is the smallest structural and functional unit of life.
**Tissue and organ** — groups of specialized cells in multicellular organisms.
**Organism (ontogenetic)** — the whole individual and its development.
**Population-species** — a group of freely interbreeding individuals of a species; the elementary unit of evolution.
**Biogeocenotic and biosphere** — exchange of matter and energy between organisms and the environment.

parts.text: Order of the levels: **“My Cat Takes Only Pure Biscuits”** — Molecule, Cell, Tissue, Organism, Population, Biosphere.

blocks.text: Stages in the development of biology

Knowledge of living nature has accumulated since ancient times: people first divided plants and animals into useful, poisonous and disease-causing groups. As data on the diversity of organisms grew, it led to the conclusion that they share a common origin. This matters for medicine: if all life has one origin, the **universal biological laws** of the whole organic world also apply to the human being as a biological object.

blocks.title: Table 1.2. Scientists who shaped biology
head: Scientist (year)
Contribution
rows: Founder of medicine; showed the role of environmental factors and heredity in disease
First classified animals; founder of zoology

“The Canon of Medicine” — the encyclopaedia of medieval medicine and biology
“On the Fabric of the Human Body” — founder of scientific anatomy
Binomial nomenclature and the foundations of taxonomy
The first complete theory of evolution
Law of embryonic similarity; founder of embryology

L. Pasteur, R. Koch, I.I. Mechnikov

blocks.text: **The biosocial nature of humans.** The human being is at the same time a biological species (*Homo sapiens*) and a social being. Human structure, reproduction, heredity, development and ageing obey general biological laws, but social factors such as lifestyle, work, diet and ecological conditions change how these laws show themselves. For example, a hereditary predisposition (diabetes mellitus, hypertension) turns into disease with an unhealthy lifestyle.

parts.text: For a physician, biology is the theoretical foundation of medicine: cell biology explains pathology, genetics explains the diagnosis of hereditary diseases and genetic counselling, the laws of ontogenesis explain congenital defects and teratogenesis, and parasitology explains the diagnosis and prevention of parasitic diseases.

sections.title: 2. The cell theory and methods of studying the cell

blocks.text: The cell was first seen in 1665 by the English scientist **R. Hooke** in a section of cork; he called it a “cell”. **A. Leeuwenhoek** observed unicellular organisms, erythrocytes and spermatozoa; **R. Brown** discovered the nucleus in 1831. In 1838–1839 **M. Schleiden** and **T. Schwann** created the cell theory, and in 1858 **R. Virchow** added the statement “Every cell comes only from a cell” (*Omnis cellula e cellula*).
Main statements of the modern cell theory

items: The cell is the elementary unit of structure, function and development of life.
The cells of all organisms are similar (homologous) in structure, chemical composition and life processes.
Cells reproduce only by division of a mother cell.
In a multicellular organism cells unite into tissues and organs and form an integrated system.
The cells of an organism are totipotent — all cells contain the same genetic information, but different genes are active in them (differentiation).

blocks.text: Important contributions to cell theory were made by **M. Malpighi** and **N. Grew** (cellular structure of plants), **J. Purkinje** (described protoplasm in 1830), **W. Flemming** (described mitosis in 1879) and **A. Weismann** (showed meiosis in germ-cell formation in 1887). After this it was confirmed that a cell consists of three parts — **the plasma membrane (or cell wall), the cytoplasm and the nucleus**.
Advantages of cellular organisation for the organism

items: Division of the body into small units increases the total surface area and speeds up metabolism.
Dead or pathologically changed cells are replaced by new ones (regeneration).
The cell stores hereditary information, doubles it (reduplication) and passes it to the next generations.
The cell stores energy, transports it and converts it into work.
In multicellular organisms the division of functions between cells (specialisation) makes evolution possible.

parts.text: In his work “Cellular Pathology”, published in 1858, R. Virchow showed that disease is the result of changes in cells. This idea founded **pathological anatomy**; modern biopsy, cytological examination (for example, the cervical smear — the Papanicolaou test) and tumour diagnosis rest on this principle.

blocks.title: Table 1.3. Methods of studying the cell
head: Method
Principle and use
rows: Viewing stained and unstained slides; resolving power ≈ 0.2 µm
Ultrastructure of organelles; resolving power ≈ 0.1–1 nm
Detecting substances in the cell (DNA, glycogen, enzymes) by color reactions
Following the path of radioactively labeled substances in the cell
Separating organelles according to their density
Growing cells outside the organism (virology, karyotype analysis)
Nuclear transfer and injection of substances into a cell with a micromanipulator

blocks.text: The light microscope consists of **mechanical**, **optical** and **illuminating** parts (Figure 1.1). The mechanical part holds all the parts together, moves the slide and adjusts the focus; the optical part magnifies the image; the illuminating part directs the light onto the slide.

blocks.label: Figure 1.1
blocks.caption: A teaching light microscope: 1 — eyepiece (ocular); 2 — body tube; 3 — revolving nosepiece; 4 — objective; 5 — stage; 6 — condenser (with diaphragm); 7 — mirror; 8 — coarse adjustment knob; 9 — fine adjustment knob; 10 — arm; 11 — base (Wikimedia Commons photograph, numbers added).

blocks.title: Table 1.4. Parts of the light microscope
head: Part
Components
Function
rows: Base, arm, body tube, revolving nosepiece, stage (with clips), coarse and fine adjustment knobs
Holds the optical parts, positions the slide, brings the image into focus
Magnifies the image of the object
Mirror (or lamp), condenser, iris diaphragm, light filter
Collects light, directs it onto the slide and controls its intensity

blocks.text: **Total magnification** = eyepiece magnification × objective magnification. For example, with a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective the object is magnified 400 times. The ×90 objective is an **immersion** objective: a drop of **cedar (immersion) oil**, whose refractive index is close to that of glass, is placed between the slide and the objective.

The quality of a microscope is determined not by its magnification but by its **resolving power** — the smallest distance at which two points are still seen as separate. In the light microscope it is about half the wavelength of light (≈ 0.2 µm); therefore small structures such as ribosomes and membranes are visible only in the electron microscope.

blocks.title: Table 1.5. Types of microscopes and microscopy
head: Type
Feature
Use
rows: Turns differences in optical density into light-dark contrast
The object appears bright on a dark background
Birefringent structures are visible in polarized light
An electron beam passes through an ultrathin section
Electrons reflected from the surface give a three-dimensional image
Surfaces of cells and tissues, surface of parasites

blocks.text: Units of measurement in microscopy and the size of objects

Cells and their parts are measured in **micrometres** (1 µm = 10^−3^ mm) and **nanometres** (1 nm = 10^−3^ µm = 10^−9^ m). The resolving power of the human eye is ≈ 0,1 mm, of the light microscope ≈ 0,2 µm and of the electron microscope ≈ 0,1–1 nm. So for each object in the table below one can predict which instrument is needed.

blocks.title: Table 1.6. Size of biological objects
head: Object
Approximate size
Means of viewing
rows: Diameter of the DNA double helix

parts.text: “**Thousand — thousand — thousand**”: 1 mm = 1000 µm, 1 µm = 1000 nm. Cells are measured in micrometres; viruses and parts of organelles in nanometres.

sections.title: 4. Rules of working with the microscope

items: Lift the microscope holding the arm with the right hand and the base with the left; place it 3–5 cm from the edge of the table with the arm facing you.
Turn the nosepiece to put the **low-power objective (×8 or ×10)** in the center until it clicks.

Raise the condenser and open the diaphragm. Looking into the eyepiece, turn the mirror until the field of view is evenly lit (with artificial light use the flat side of the mirror, with daylight — the concave side).
Put the slide on the stage with the coverslip facing up, fix it with the clips and bring the area to be studied under the objective.

Looking from the side, lower the objective with the coarse adjustment knob to 0.5 cm above the slide; then, looking into the eyepiece, turn the knob **away from yourself** (raising the tube) until a clear image appears.

Bring the area of interest to the center of the field and switch the nosepiece to the **high-power objective (×40)**; sharpen the image only with the **fine adjustment knob** (turning it no more than half a turn).
After work put the low-power objective in place, remove the slide, wipe the microscope with a soft cloth and put it in its case.

parts.text: The **coarse adjustment knob** must not be used with the high-power objective: its working distance is about 0.6 mm, so it touches the slide, breaks the coverslip and damages the lens. Do not wipe lenses with your fingers or with paper.

blocks.text: **Drawing rule:** the slide is viewed with the left eye while both eyes stay open; the drawing is made with the right hand in an album with a simple pencil, the parts are named with pointer lines, and the name of the slide and the magnification are written under the drawing.
Working with the immersion objective (×90)

items: First view the preparation with the low-power and then the high-power objective and bring the area of interest to the centre of the field.
Turn the revolver to move the objective aside and put one drop of immersion (cedar) oil on that spot of the preparation.
Looking from the side, carefully lower the immersion objective until it dips into the oil drop.
Raise the condenser to the top position and open the diaphragm fully — immersion needs a lot of light.
Looking into the eyepiece, focus the image with the micrometer screw only.
After work, wipe the oil off the objective and the preparation at once with a soft cloth moistened with benzine or xylene.

blocks.title: Table 1.7. Typical problems when working with the microscope
head: Problem
Probable cause
Correction
rows: The field of view is dark
The objective has not clicked into place; diaphragm closed; condenser lowered
Set the revolver, open the diaphragm, raise the condenser, adjust the mirror
The image is blurred, like a “fog”
Dirty lens or eyepiece; preparation placed upside down
Wipe the lens with a special cloth; the coverslip must face upwards
Half of the field is lit
The objective is not turned fully into place
Turn the revolver until it clicks
Spots that move in the field
Rotate the eyepiece; if the spot also turns, clean the eyepiece
No image is found at high power
The object was not centred; focusing was done with the coarse screw
Return to low power, centre the object, then use the fine screw

blocks.text: A **temporary slide** is prepared in a drop of water, glycerol or saline for viewing during one class; it dries quickly and cannot be stored for long. A **permanent slide** is prepared by fixing the tissue, dehydrating it, embedding it in paraffin, cutting it on a microtome into sections 5–7 µm thick, staining it (for example, with hematoxylin and eosin) and mounting it under Canada balsam; it can be kept for many years.
Preparing a temporary slide of onion skin epidermis

items: Place 1 drop of water in the middle of a clean glass slide with a pipette.
With forceps peel a thin, transparent film of epidermis from the inner concave surface of an onion scale.
Spread the film in the drop, making sure it does not fold.
Touch the drop with the coverslip held at an angle of 45° and lower it slowly — this way no air bubbles remain.

Remove the excess water with filter paper; if needed, put a drop of iodine solution at the edge of the coverslip and draw it under with filter paper from the opposite side (the nucleus stains yellow-brown).
Examine the slide first under low power and then under high power, and draw the cell wall, cytoplasm, nucleus and vacuole.

parts.text: Round “cells” with a thick black rim on a slide are often **air bubbles**: when the focus knob is turned, their black rim widens and narrows, while a real cell shows an internal structure (the nucleus).

blocks.text: Stages of making a permanent preparation

items: **Fixation** — preserving cell structures close to their living state in formalin, alcohol or Carnoy's fluid.
**Washing** — rinsing the fixative out with water.
**Dehydration** — removing water in alcohols of increasing strength (70°, 80°, 96°, absolute).
**Clearing** — making the tissue transparent in xylene or chloroform.
**Embedding** — immersing in melted paraffin to form a solid block.
**Sectioning** — cutting sections 5–7 µm thick on a microtome.
**Staining** — removing the paraffin and staining the section (haematoxylin-eosin).
**Mounting** — covering the section with a coverslip over a drop of Canada balsam.

blocks.text: Temporary preparation of human buccal epithelium

items: Gently scrape the inner surface of the cheek with a sterile spatula or toothpick.
Smear the material into one drop of physiological saline on a slide.
Add one drop of methylene blue (or iodine) solution and cover with a coverslip.
At low and high power, observe and draw the flat, polygonal cells and the round nucleus in their centre.

blocks.title: Table 1.8. Stains used for microscopic preparations
head: Stain
What it stains (colour)
rows: Blood cells, malaria plasmodium — nucleus red, cytoplasm blue
DNA — crimson-violet (a cytochemical reaction specific to DNA)

sections.title: 6. The non-cellular form of life — viruses and bacteriophages

blocks.text: Viruses were discovered in 1892 by the Russian scientist **D.I. Ivanovsky** while studying tobacco mosaic disease. Viruses are **obligate intracellular parasites** 20–300 nm in size that reproduce only inside living cells. Outside the cell (as a virion) they show no properties of life, but after entering a cell they carry out their own genetic program; that is why they are regarded as a form between living and non-living nature.

blocks.label: Figure 1.2
blocks.caption: Viruses of various shapes: herpes virus (icosahedral capsid and envelope), influenza virus (helical nucleocapsid and envelope), tobacco mosaic virus (helical symmetry) and a bacteriophage (complex symmetry) (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Structure of a virus

items: **Nucleic acid** (the genome) — either DNA or RNA (never both); single- or double-stranded.
**Capsid** — the protein coat surrounding the nucleic acid; built of capsomeres. Nucleic acid + capsid = **nucleocapsid**.
**Envelope** (supercapsid) — in complex viruses, a lipoprotein membrane taken from the host cell membrane, carrying glycoprotein “spikes” (influenza, HIV, herpes).
Some viruses carry enzymes: for example, HIV has **reverse transcriptase**, which makes a DNA copy of RNA.

blocks.label: Figure 1.3
blocks.caption: Structure of the human immunodeficiency virus (HIV): lipid envelope with glycoprotein “spikes”, protein coat (capsid), RNA and the enzyme reverse transcriptase (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Viruses exist in two forms: the **extracellular (resting) form** — the virion, which shows no signs of life; and the **intracellular (reproducing) form** — the virus–cell complex. By structure, **simple viruses** (only nucleic acid and a protein capsid) and **complex viruses** (with an additional lipoprotein envelope, carbohydrates and enzymes) are distinguished.

blocks.title: Table 1.9. Groups of viruses by genome
head: Group
Examples
rows: Smallpox, herpesviruses (herpes simplex, chickenpox, Epstein–Barr), adenoviruses, papillomaviruses

blocks.text: Reproduction of a virus in the cell

items: **Adsorption** — the virus binds to a specific receptor on the cell surface.
**Entry** — by endocytosis or membrane fusion; a bacteriophage injects only its nucleic acid.
**Uncoating** — the capsid breaks down and the genome is released.
**Synthesis** — viral nucleic acid and proteins are made using the cell’s machinery.
**Assembly** — new virions are formed.
**Release** — by lysis of the cell or by budding.

blocks.text: **Bacteriophages** (phages) are viruses that parasitize bacteria; they were discovered in 1917 by F. d’Hérelle. A phage consists of a head (DNA inside an icosahedral capsid), a tail (a contractile sheath and an inner tube), a base plate and tail fibers (Figure 1.4). **Virulent** phages lyse the bacterium; **temperate** phages insert their DNA into the bacterial chromosome (a prophage), produce lysogeny and carry genes in transduction. Phages are used to treat intestinal infections (phage therapy) and to type bacteria.

blocks.label: Figure 1.4
blocks.caption: Structure of a bacteriophage: head (DNA inside the capsid), tail, base plate and tail fibers; on the right — phages attached to the surface of a bacterium as seen in the electron microscope (P.Kh. Kholikov et al., 2022).

blocks.label: Figure 1.5
blocks.caption: Reproduction cycle of a bacteriophage in a bacterial cell: adsorption and injection of DNA, synthesis of phage DNA and proteins, assembly of new phages and lysis of the bacterium (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.title: Table 1.10. Lytic and lysogenic cycles
head: Feature
Lytic cycle
Lysogenic cycle
rows: Lyses in 20–40 minutes, releasing up to 100–200 new phages
Survives and passes the prophage to its progeny
Phage therapy, phage typing of bacteria
Transduction; appearance of new properties (for example, the diphtheria toxin gene is carried by a prophage)

blocks.title: Table 1.11. Important viral diseases of humans
head: Disease
Agent (genome)
Main site affected
Route of transmission
rows: Motor neurons of the spinal cord

parts.text: Antibiotics do not act on viruses because viruses have no cell wall, no ribosomes and no metabolism of their own. The main measures against viral infections are **vaccination** and **antiviral drugs** acting on the stages of viral reproduction (for example, reverse transcriptase inhibitors in HIV infection).

blocks.text: Hypotheses on the origin of viruses

items: **Regressive hypothesis** — viruses arose by simplification (degeneration) of microorganisms that turned to a parasitic way of life.
**Organelle hypothesis** — viruses originated from cell organelles or autonomous genetic elements (episomes, plasmids).
**“Escaped genes” hypothesis** — viruses are fragments of normal genes that broke away from the cell and gained the ability to multiply on their own.

blocks.text: Prions and viroids

There are infectious agents even simpler than viruses. **Prions** are misfolded **protein** particles without any nucleic acid; they convert the normal prion protein into a pathological form like themselves (S. Prusiner, 1982). Prions cause fatal brain diseases such as Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease, kuru and “mad cow disease” (spongiform encephalopathy); they resist boiling, alcohol and ultraviolet light. **Viroids** are small circular RNA molecules of 250–400 nucleotides with no protein coat; they cause disease mainly in plants (T. Diener, 1971).

parts.text: Prions are not destroyed by ordinary sterilisation regimens, so neurosurgical instruments are decontaminated by enhanced methods (prolonged autoclaving at 134 °C, alkaline solutions) or disposable instruments are used.

blocks.text: Cellular organisms are divided into two groups. **Prokaryotes** (*pro* — before, *karyon* — nucleus) are bacteria and archaea without a formed nucleus. **Eukaryotes** are the cells of fungi, plants, animals and humans that have a true nucleus.

A **bacterial cell** is 0.5–5 µm in size. It consists of a cell wall (peptidoglycan — murein), sometimes a capsule, the cytoplasmic membrane and its folds — **mesosomes**, cytoplasm, **70S ribosomes**, a **nucleoid** (a single circular DNA molecule) and **plasmids** (additional small circular DNA). Most have flagella and pili (fimbriae). By shape, cocci, rods (bacilli), vibrios and spirilla are distinguished. Bacteria reproduce by **binary fission**; under favorable conditions they divide every 20–30 minutes. Under unfavorable conditions some of them form **spores**.

blocks.label: Figure 1.6
blocks.caption: Structure of a bacterial cell. Left — a model based on electron microscopy, right — an electron micrograph of the bacterium *Salmonella*: 1 — flagellum; 2 — cell wall; 3 — cytoplasmic membrane; 4 — nucleoid; 5 — plasmid; 6 — mesosome; 7 — cytoplasm; 8 — ribosomes (P.X. Xolikov et al., 2022).

blocks.text: Bacteria have no true sexual reproduction, but **exchange of genetic information** (parasexual processes) does occur. Through these processes, for example, antibiotic-resistance genes spread rapidly:

items: **Conjugation** — two bacteria connect by a cytoplasmic bridge (sex pilus) and transfer a plasmid or part of the chromosome.
**Transformation** — a bacterium takes up a free DNA fragment from the environment (F. Griffith, 1928, pneumococcus experiment).
**Transduction** — a DNA fragment is carried from one bacterium to another by a bacteriophage.

blocks.text: A **spore** is a resting form produced under unfavourable conditions (drought, high temperature): a thick, multilayered coat forms around the chromosome and the rest of the cell dies. Spores remain viable for decades, survive boiling and are killed only in an autoclave (120 °C, under pressure). By their relation to oxygen, bacteria are **aerobic**, **anaerobic** (the agents of tetanus and gas gangrene) or **facultatively anaerobic** (*E. coli*).

**Mycoplasmas** are the smallest free-living prokaryotes, 0.1–0.3 µm in size, without a cell wall; their shape is variable and they are not sensitive to penicillin (they cause pneumonia and urogenital infections).

blocks.title: Table 1.12. Main differences between prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells
head: Feature
Prokaryotes
Eukaryotes
rows: Absent; DNA lies in the cytoplasm (nucleoid)
One circular DNA without histones; plasmids
Several linear chromosomes, DNA bound to histones
ER, Golgi complex, mitochondria, lysosomes, plastids

Simple, made of the protein flagellin

parts.text: The presence of circular DNA and 70S ribosomes in mitochondria and plastids shows that they originated from ancient prokaryotes (**symbiogenesis theory**).

blocks.title: Table 1.13. Important diseases caused by bacteria
head: Disease
Agent
Route of transmission
rows: Raw milk, meat, contact with animals

blocks.text: Most scientists consider that eukaryotic cells arose from prokaryotes. Two main theories explain the origin of the eukaryotic cell and its organelles.

**Invagination theory** — internal membrane systems, the nuclear envelope, the ER and other membrane organelles formed as a result of the inward folding (invagination) of the prokaryotic cell membrane. This theory explains well why the nuclear envelope and the ER form one membrane system.

**Symbiosis (endosymbiosis) theory** (L. Margulis, 1967) — a large anaerobic cell living by fermentation engulfed aerobic bacteria by phagocytosis but did not digest them; this mutually beneficial coexistence became hereditary. The aerobic bacteria became **mitochondria** (their ancestors are purple bacteria), and photosynthetic cyanobacteria became **chloroplasts**.
Evidence supporting the symbiosis theory

items: Mitochondria and chloroplasts have **two membranes**; the composition of the inner membrane resembles the bacterial membrane.
They contain histone-free **circular DNA** and their own genes.
They have **70S ribosomes** like those of bacteria; some antibiotics that act on bacteria (chloramphenicol) also stop protein synthesis in mitochondria.
They multiply independently of the cell by **binary fission**.
Mitochondrial rRNA is close to that of purple bacteria, and chloroplast rRNA to that of cyanobacteria.

blocks.text: By comparing the nucleotide sequences of ribosomal RNA, C. Woese (1977) divided all cellular organisms into three domains — **Bacteria (eubacteria)**, **Archaea (archaebacteria)** and **Eukaryotes**. Because their genetic code is the same, the hypothesis of a common ancestor — the **progenote** — was put forward.

parts.text: Mitochondria are passed only through the mother (with the cytoplasm of the egg), so diseases caused by mitochondrial DNA mutations (for example, Leber hereditary optic neuropathy) are transmitted only from the mother to all her children. The ototoxic effect of some antibiotics acting on bacterial ribosomes (aminoglycosides) is also linked to the similarity of mitochondrial ribosomes to bacterial ones.

skills.title: Skill: examining a slide under the low-power and high-power objective

items: Place the microscope correctly and put the low-power objective into working position.
Raise the condenser, open the diaphragm and light the field of view with the mirror.
Put the slide on the stage with the coverslip facing up and fix it.
Looking from the side, lower the objective with the coarse knob to 0.5 cm.
Looking into the eyepiece, raise the tube and find a clear image.
Bring the area of interest to the center and switch the nosepiece to the ×40 objective.
Adjust the sharpness only with the fine adjustment knob.
Calculate the total magnification and draw the picture in the album.

skills.title: Skill: preparing and staining a temporary slide

items: Put 1 drop of water on a glass slide.
Separate the object (onion epidermis) and spread it in the drop.
Lower the coverslip slowly at an angle of 45°.
Remove the excess water with filter paper.
Put the stain (iodine solution) at the edge of the coverslip and draw it under with filter paper from the opposite side.
Examine the slide under the microscope and identify the parts of the cell.

skills.title: Skill: preparing and staining a human buccal epithelium smear

items: Put 1 drop of physiological saline on a slide.
Take a gentle scraping from the inner surface of the cheek with a sterile spatula and smear it into the drop.
Add 1 drop of methylene blue and wait 1–2 minutes.
Lower the coverslip at a 45° angle and remove excess fluid with filter paper.
Find a group of cells at low power and look at a single cell at high power.
Draw the cell membrane, cytoplasm and nucleus and write the magnification; put the used spatula into disinfectant solution.

cases.title: Case 1
cases.text: A student saw the slide well under the low-power objective, then switched the nosepiece to the high-power objective, but the image disappeared.
cases.ask: What are the possible causes, and how should they be corrected?
cases.answer: Causes: (1) the area of interest was not brought to the center of the field — the field of the high-power objective is much narrower; (2) the slide is upside down (coverslip facing down), so the high-power objective cannot reach focus; (3) there is not enough light — with the high-power objective the diaphragm must be opened and the condenser raised; (4) the objective was not turned until it clicked into place. Correction: return to the low-power objective, center the area, place the slide correctly, increase the light and adjust only with the fine knob.

cases.title: Case 2
cases.text: A student broke the coverslip while working with the high-power objective.
cases.answer: The sharpness under the high-power objective was adjusted with the coarse knob: the working distance of this objective is very small (≈ 0.6 mm), so with the coarse knob the tube drops sharply and the objective hits the slide. The slide may also have been placed upside down. The correct way is to use only the fine adjustment knob with the high-power objective and to bring the objective close to the slide while looking from the side.

cases.title: Case 3
cases.text: In a light microscope slide, cells were seen whose flattened nucleus was pressed to the edge of the cell and whose cytoplasm consisted of one large cavity.
cases.ask: What cell could this be? Why is the nucleus pushed to the edge?
cases.answer: This could be a fat cell (adipocyte) or a mature plant cell with a large central vacuole. In an adipocyte almost all the cytoplasm is occupied by a single large fat droplet; in a plant cell, by the central vacuole filled with cell sap. In both cases the large inclusion or vacuole presses the nucleus and the cytoplasm against the cell wall (to the periphery).

cases.title: Case 4
cases.text: A student tried to look at bacteria with a ×10 eyepiece and a ×40 objective, but they looked like tiny dots and the student could not make out their structure.
cases.ask: What magnification is needed and how can it be achieved?
cases.answer: With the ×40 objective the total magnification is 10 × 40 = 400 times — not enough for a bacterium (0,5–5 µm). Bacteria are examined with the **immersion objective** (×90): total magnification 10 × 90 = 900 times. For this, a drop of immersion oil is put on the preparation, the objective is dipped into the oil, the condenser is raised and the diaphragm fully opened, and focusing is done only with the fine screw. Because the oil has the same refractive index as glass, light rays are not scattered and the resolving power increases.

cases.title: Case 5
cases.text: A patient came to the doctor with symptoms of a cold (fever, blocked nose, cough) and demanded an antibiotic. Examination showed an acute respiratory viral infection.
cases.ask: Will an antibiotic be effective here? Justify your answer by the structure of viruses and bacteria.
cases.answer: No. Antibiotics act on structures typical of bacteria — the cell wall (peptidoglycan), 70S ribosomes and bacterial enzymes. Viruses have no cell wall, no ribosomes and no independent metabolism: they use the machinery of the host cell. So an antibiotic does not act on a virus; instead it disturbs the normal microflora and selects resistant bacteria. An antibiotic is prescribed only when a bacterial complication (for example, bacterial pneumonia) develops.

cases.title: Case 6
cases.text: In a hospital, resistance to an antibiotic appeared in one strain of *E. coli*. A few weeks later the same resistance was found in another species of intestinal bacteria (*Klebsiella*).
cases.ask: How could the resistance gene have passed from one species to another?
cases.answer: Resistance genes are often located on **plasmids**. A plasmid passes between bacteria by **conjugation** (through the sex pilus), even between different species. The gene can also pass by **transduction** (with a bacteriophage) or **transformation** (uptake of free DNA from the environment). This is why unjustified use of antibiotics leads to rapid spread of resistant strains.

summary.label: Remember
summary.text: Work with the microscope always starts with the **low-power objective**; with the high-power objective only the **fine adjustment knob** is used.

summary.label: Memory aid
summary.text: Structure of a virus “from inside out”: **Genome → Capsid → Envelope** (“GCE — Get Coat, Envelope”).

summary.label: Clinical significance
summary.text: The 70S ribosomes and peptidoglycan wall of bacteria are the targets of antibiotics; because human cells lack them, antibiotics act selectively — and they do not act on viruses.
